Lesson1.6-the-engineers-seat 1.6-the-engineers-seat

The lifecycle it keeps

Engineering ran on the same handful of activities long before software, and software inherits them whole: **requirements**, **specification**, **design**, **implementation** (for software, writing the code), **validation**, and **maintenance**.

The two seats

Two words for two jobs, and this book keeps them apart.

SDLC to SELC

The field's own name for the lifecycle gives the old arrangement away: SDLC, the software *development* life cycle.

A different seat is a different discipline

Same lifecycle, then; no new phases.

Lesson2.5-the-logical-view 2.5-the-logical-view

The service-flow / API model

*The typed source-of-truth for a service-oriented architecture — its services, their endpoints, their authentication, and the wiring between them — from which the access policy and environment wiring are generated and against which the real call graph is checked.*

The domain registries

**Freeze engineering facts that change slowly but are consulted everywhere.** A fact read in many places and revised rarely is exactly the fact that drifts when each reader keeps its own copy; make it a registry every consumer joins to by key, and disagreement becomes a build failure instead of a latent inconsistency.

Lesson2.6-the-process-view 2.6-the-process-view

Formal invariant verification: the verification backbone

Formal invariant verification is the backbone the three models hang their invariant tables on — a governance method over the models, not a model of the running system.

The synchronization model

*A typed registry that models the system's synchronization behavior — every OS-level lock, which shared resource it guards, and the required acquisition ordering — so concurrency contracts are declared and checkable, not tribal.*

Two ways to make a concurrent write safe: the mediator and the single-writer registries

The synchronization model catalogs the raw locks.

The mediator registry

The mediator registry is the *how-many* half.

The single-writer registry

The single-writer registry is the *exactly-one* half, and its failure mode is what makes it a separate model.

Lesson2.7-the-development-view 2.7-the-development-view

The component & zone model

*A typed catalog of every component's code zone — its focus directories, its tags, its boundary kind, its external seams, its read surfaces — so "which component owns this file, and what may touch it" is a queried fact rather than a per-tool guess.*

The rule-metadata registry

The rule-metadata registry is the self-referential slice of the domain registries: the governance rules' own metadata, and so a model the governance machinery — and this book — are partly governed by.

Lesson2.8-the-physical-view 2.8-the-physical-view

The performance/cost view: mostly embodied, one honest gap

The zoo names a performance and cost model as a general type, and the framework supports it.

The deployment & tier topology model

*The typed statement of where things run — each service's name, its layer, and its tier — from which the deploy scripts and layering lints reason about a declared topology rather than scattered constants, and against which the real deploy table is reconciled.*

The invariant-DAG execution policy

The insight is one sentence: **correctness dependencies stay in the graph; host-specific resource limits live in a scheduler profile.** What must be true on *every* host — B is wrong without A — belongs in the deploy graph.

The control↔substrate dependency model

The substrate-dependency model makes each governance mechanism declare, as typed metadata, the substrate assumption it bakes in — bound to one substrate, substrate-aware, or substrate-agnostic.

Lesson2.9-the-scenarios-view 2.9-the-scenarios-view

The user-journey model

The user-journey model makes the product's journeys first-class typed entities — each an actor pursuing a goal through ordered steps, every boundary-crossing step joined to the endpoint it calls.

The agent-orchestration model

The agent-orchestration model is the developer-journey counterpart — the scenarios view pointed at the fleet rather than the user.

Journey-criticality → test-placement

This model — the **Selector** in the join below — derives which environment tier a journey's tests run in from the journey's criticality: a `MAJOR` part runs the fast local tier and the full staging matrix, a `MINOR` part runs staging only.

Coverage → model-node mapping

Coverage-to-node mapping projects the test suite's coverage onto the model's *nodes* — states, seams, invariants, journey endpoints — instead of its lines (node coverage over line coverage, as [Metrics](3.5-metrics.html) laid out).

Journey task-closure — asserting the goal completed

The three models above ask whether a journey's test *exists*, *runs*, and runs *in which tier*.

Worked join — the journey↔coverage↔deploy-policy composition

**The compositional question:** *watch one fact — a journey is* major — *travel through four models with nothing said twice, until a product goal reaches all the way to how the deploy rations its tests.* The other model pages each show a single model; this one shows them **joining, not repeating.** Four models compose on one shared key — the journey and its endpoints:

The three questions the join answers

Three questions the raw deploy scripts and test config cannot answer on their own.

The composite picture

Everything so far has examined models individually.

The invariants the join spans

The join's invariants span all four models, collected in [ref:scenarios-invariants].

The Selector and Scheduler in code

Two pieces of real policy code make the join concrete — the **Selector** derives a host's test roster from the journey model, and the **Scheduler** rations that roster per host.

Tracing one fact through four models

The join keys chain, and a reader can walk them against the figure: the **endpoint** ties M13 to M5, the **criticality** ties M13 to M6, the **derived tier** ties M6 to M7's roster, and the **host profile** ties the roster to the plan.

Lesson4.1-the-mage-workflow 4.1-the-mage-workflow

The loop, one turn at a time

**Need.** A turn begins with something you want to be true — a feature to ship, a property to guarantee, a class of bug to end.

Closing the loop: governance conversion

When a check goes red, the reflex the method trains is not to patch the instance but to close the class it belongs to.

From soft to hard

How much governance is enough

Which raises the real question: how much governance is enough?

Example — Spotify Migration at fleet scale stays incremental: you target a change, schedule it across the estate, drain it, and keep a human on the exceptions. Spotify is the evidence it holds at organizational size — a fleet-wide migration that once drew in hundreds of teams and ran for weeks is now scoped by one engineer over a few days, the tooling targeting and scheduling the work while agents implement it concurrently and the engineer watches the fleet and handles the exceptions rather than typing each change [cite:spotify2026honk]. What to imitate is the placement, not the tool: put the scarce human decision upstream — *what, where, when, whether* — and let the environment carry the change onward, the same move the strategies above run at a single-subsystem grain. The takeaway is that scale does not undo the incremental discipline; it raises the payoff, so the move that repays weeks on one subsystem repays far more across a fleet.

What does it mean to validate a change?

To validate a change is to assemble evidence that it satisfies its obligations — and to refuse it otherwise.

Validation from executable models

The move: a generator hunts a counterexample to a model

After this section — the reader can

Fuzz + MBSE: the structured model becomes the oracle

The richest form of validation-from-a-model turns the model itself into the judge.

Validation from engineering metrics

A validator answers a yes/no obligation; a **metric** answers a question of degree, and degree is its own kind of evidence.

Deterministic validators

Models expose intent and metrics measure degree; **validators** are the machine-read checks that consume both and return a verdict.

Property-based testing: the invariant is the oracle

In property-based testing the author writes the law and the machine hunts the counterexample.

Fuzzing: the contract is "never crash, never corrupt"

Property testing asks a rich question of inputs drawn from an authored domain.

When to reach for which

The family gives a compact decision aid, and the axes of the opening table are the decision.

Lesson5.1-the-ada-context 5.1-the-ada-context

A noble idea with a crushing implementation

The Americans with Disabilities Act starts from a simple promise: people with disabilities should have equal access to public life — to work, travel, study, vote, and use services without barriers society could reasonably remove.

The rule that changed the burden

Universities have owed Title II compliance since 1990, but for most of that time they complied reactively: a student hit an inaccessible document, requested an accommodation, and the institution scrambled to respond.

What it costs to make one document accessible

Compliance carries a cost, and the cost is easiest to feel on a single deck.

Why a document is not just a file

Underneath the institutional bind sits a technical problem deeper than it looks — the reason this became a software project worth building rather than a policy memo worth writing.
